Nobody ever announced that belief into your conscious mind. It just sat there, under it, as a Catholic schoolroom rule most people stopped quoting decades ago - which doesn't mean it stopped working. Kevin's point: having money got filed as 'of the devil.' Staying broke got filed as 'of God.' That's not a thought you think. That's a program running underneath the thoughts you think.

clips.send: Send this to a friend who says they want more money but somehow never seems to let it in - the uneasy click of finally seeing why.
clips.caption:
Say out loud, 'money is good.' Now say, 'money is bad.' One of those two sentences will feel more true in your body than the other - and it might not be the one you'd pick with your conscious mind.

That gap is the whole lesson. You can believe, logically, that money is good: it pays your bills, it protects your family. But if an older belief is still sitting underneath that logic, your body will quietly disagree with you every time you say it.

Kevin's fix is almost insultingly simple: say 'having money is good' on purpose, every day, until your body stops arguing with you.

clips.caption:
Before a political ad ever reaches your TV, it's already been tested on a room full of strangers wired up to monitors - heart rate, temperature, the works. Not to see if they liked it. To see if it worked on them.

Kevin says he sat in those rooms. The phrase, the tie, the tone of voice - none of it is improvised. It's reverse-engineered from your own nervous system's reaction, then aimed back at you.

You don't have to pick a side to see this clearly. You just have to know the ad was never trying to inform you. It was trying to move you, and it already knew exactly how.
